wstep: This card describes fruit leather from apricots using the general NCHFP recipe: a thin layer of purée is dried at 140 °F (60 °C) in a dehydrator or oven and rolled up.

akapity: NCHFP does not describe qamar al-din: this card applies the general NCHFP recipe for fruit leather from fresh fruit to apricots, not the traditional way of making qamar al-din.
Select ripe or slightly overripe fruit; wash it in cool water, remove the peel, seeds and stem and cut it into chunks.
Discard any fruit that shows decay, bruises or mould: such defects can affect all of the dried product.
Purée the fruit until smooth; 2 cups of fruit make a 13 × 15-inch (about 33 × 38 cm) leather.
Purée from light-coloured fruit darkens: for every 2 cups of light-coloured fruit add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice or 1/8 teaspoon (375 mg) of ascorbic acid.
Sweetening is optional: for each 2 cups of fruit add 1/4–1/2 cup of sugar, corn syrup or honey.
For longer storage, corn syrup or honey is best because it prevents crystals; sugar is fine for immediate use or short storage.
In an oven, use a 13 × 15-inch (about 33 × 38 cm) cookie pan with edges lined with plastic wrap; smooth out the wrinkles.
Do not use waxed paper or aluminium foil.
In a dehydrator, use specially designed plastic sheets or line plastic trays with plastic wrap.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Spread the purée evenly about 1/8 inch (about 3 mm) thick, not too close to the edge of the pan.
Dry the leather at 140 °F (60 °C).
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the fruit cooks instead of drying.
Check the oven temperature: place a calibrated oven thermometer on the rack or tray and check it every 2 hours throughout drying.
Leave the oven door open 2–3 inches (about 5–7.5 cm) so moisture can escape.
Larger leathers take longer to dry; approximate drying times are 6–8 hours in a dehydrator and up to 18 hours in an oven.
The leather dries from the outside edge toward the centre; it is dry when touching the centre leaves no indentation.
While still warm, peel the leather from the plastic and roll it up, let it cool and rewrap the roll in plastic.
Pack only completely cooled rolls: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the dried fruit in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried fruit to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store the dried fruit in a cool, dry, dark place.
Fruit leather keeps up to 1 month at room temperature and up to 1 year in the freezer, tightly wrapped.
This card does not cover fillings; if you spread the dried leather with, for example, cream cheese, cheese spread, peanut butter, chocolate or jam and roll it, store such rolls in the refrigerator.
Check the dried fruit often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy dried fruit; also throw away dried fruit that smells off.
